# Development Mode

> Activated by `/mode dev`. This is the default.

## Behavior

- Write code first, explain after
- Prefer a working solution over a perfect one
- Run `verification-loop` after every change, not at the end
- Keep commits atomic
- Echo the user's input and the active repo at the top of every response

## Priorities, In Order

1. **Get it working** — the minimal viable change
2. **Get it right** — handle the edge cases the user actually mentioned
3. **Get it clean** — refactor only when asked

The order is the whole point. Reversing it produces beautiful code that does not do the
thing.

## Tools To Favor

- String-replacement edits for code changes
- Terminal for build and test
- Grep and glob to locate, then read the narrowed range
- The structural graph before re-exploring the tree

## Tools To Avoid

- Broad semantic search — too diffuse for implementation work
- Large parallel fans — reserve them for genuinely multi-file reads

## Quality Gate

- Build passes
- New code includes or updates tests **when a test file already exists** for that unit
- No new lint errors

## Skip

- Architecture justification — that is review mode
- Multi-paragraph commentary on a three-line change
- Speculative future-proofing for a second case that does not exist

## Token Discipline

Read narrowly before you read widely. Grep to locate, then read the range — opening a
whole file to find one function is the most common avoidable cost in this system.

- Prefer the structural graph (`python scripts/graph.py`) over re-exploring the tree.
  It exists so you spend roughly two thousand tokens on a symbol summary instead of
  re-reading source you already indexed.
- Reference material in a skill's `references/` folder loads **on demand only**. Do not
  pull one in unless the task needs it.
- When you trim or truncate anything, say so with an explicit marker. Continuing past a
  cut as though you had read the remainder is a named failure mode, not an accident.

The reason for the discipline: discovery-tier cost is paid by every user, in every
repo, on every conversation, before anyone types anything. A kilobyte saved there is
worth far more than a kilobyte saved in a response nobody re-reads.
